title: Working Scientifically in Chemistry
description: Variables, hypotheses, planning experiments, data types, graphs and evaluation — the practical skills of KS3 chemistry.

notes.heading: Independent, Dependent and Control Variables
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A variable is any factor that can change or be measured during an experiment. Every investigation has three kinds:
• Independent variable — the one thing you deliberately change.
• Dependent variable — the thing you measure; it may change in response.
• Control variables — all the other factors you keep the same.

🔑 How it works
An experiment tests how the independent variable affects the dependent variable. If a control variable is allowed to change as well, you cannot be sure what caused your results, so the test is no longer valid (a fair test).

💡 Worked Example
A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the time taken for a strip of magnesium to disappear.
• Independent variable: the concentration of the acid.
• Dependent variable: the time for the magnesium to disappear.
• Control variables: the volume of acid, the temperature, and the size and mass of the magnesium strip.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Change ONE thing, measure ONE thing, keep everything else the same.
• List your control variables and say HOW you will keep each one constant.
• The dependent variable is usually measured with an instrument (stopwatch, thermometer, balance).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up the independent and dependent variables. Ask yourself: "What am I changing on purpose?" — that is the independent variable. What you then measure is the dependent variable.

notes.heading: Hypotheses and Predictions
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• A hypothesis is an idea, based on scientific knowledge, that explains how or why something happens. It must be testable by experiment.
• A prediction is a statement of what you expect to happen in the experiment if the hypothesis is correct.

🔑 How it works
A prediction links the independent variable to the dependent variable: it says how one will change when the other changes. Predictions are often written in the form "If ... then ... because ...", where the "because" part gives the scientific reason.

💡 Worked Example
Hypothesis: Reactions go faster when the reacting particles collide more often.
Prediction: If the temperature of the acid is increased, then the time for the magnesium ribbon to disappear will decrease, because warmer particles move faster and collide more often.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A hypothesis explains; a prediction states what you expect to observe.
• A prediction must mention both the independent and dependent variables.
• After the experiment, you compare your results with the prediction to decide whether the hypothesis is supported.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a prediction that does not link the variables, such as "the experiment will work" or "the reaction will be interesting". A prediction must say how the dependent variable will change.

notes.heading: Planning an Experiment and Writing a Method
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A method is a description of how an experiment is carried out, usually written as a numbered list of instructions. A good plan turns a scientific question into a method that produces accurate and precise data.

🔑 How it works
Plan an experiment in five steps:
1. Ask the question — state what you want to find out (a hypothesis can help).
2. Identify the variables — name the independent and dependent variables, list the control variables and how you will keep them constant.
3. Make a prediction — say what you expect to happen, and why.
4. List the equipment — name all the apparatus you need.
5. Write the method — a numbered list of steps, one action per step.

💡 Worked Example
A step in a method for heating water might read: "Measure $50 \text{ cm}^3$ of water into a beaker using a measuring cylinder, then place the beaker on a tripod and gauze above a Bunsen burner." Notice it names the apparatus, gives quantities, and describes one clear action.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Use the proper scientific names for apparatus (conical flask, not "conical beaker").
• Include quantities: volumes, masses, temperatures and times.
• Someone else should be able to follow your method and get similar results — that is the test of a good method.
• A labelled diagram of the set-up can make the method clearer.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing steps that are too vague, like "heat the water and see what happens". Without quantities and named apparatus, nobody can repeat the experiment.

notes.heading: Hazards, Risks and Working Safely
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• A hazard is something that can cause harm, such as a corrosive acid or a Bunsen flame.
• A risk is the chance that the hazard will actually cause harm.

🔑 How it works
Chemicals that are hazardous carry a hazard symbol on their label — a diamond-shaped warning sign showing the type of harm (for example corrosive, flammable or toxic). You cannot remove a hazard like concentrated acid, but you can reduce the risk by taking precautions.

💡 Worked Example
When heating dilute hydrochloric acid, the hazards are the acid (corrosive) and the hot apparatus (burns). Precautions that reduce the risk include wearing safety goggles, standing up while working, tying back long hair, and pointing the test tube away from people.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always follow the lab rules: no eating or drinking, never run, never taste or sniff chemicals directly, and follow the instructions of the person in charge.
• Keep bags and coats out of the way and tuck stools under benches to avoid trips.
• Wear goggles whenever you handle chemicals or heat anything.
• Tell the teacher straight away about any spillage or breakage.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing hazard and risk. The acid is the hazard — that does not change. Wearing goggles and gloves reduces the RISK of it harming you; it does not remove the hazard.

notes.heading: Types of Data
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Data is the information collected in an investigation — the measurements and observations you record.
• Qualitative data is described in words (e.g. "the solution turned blue").
• Quantitative data is described in numbers (e.g. "the temperature rose by $12$ °C").

🔑 How it works
Quantitative variables come in two kinds, and there is also a word-based kind:
• Continuous — can take any value within a range, such as temperature, time, mass or volume.
• Discrete — can only take certain values, usually whole numbers, such as the number of bubbles produced or the number of people.
• Categoric — the values are words or labels, such as the colour of a precipitate (red, blue, green) or the type of metal used.

💡 Worked Example
In an experiment reacting different metals with acid:
• The metal used (magnesium, zinc, iron) is categoric.
• The number of gas bubbles counted is discrete.
• The temperature rise of the acid is continuous.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The dependent variable is often continuous, but not always.
• Deciding what type of data you have helps you choose the right table, chart or graph later.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking discrete data can have decimal values. A count (like bubbles or drops) can only be a whole number, so it is discrete — even though it is numeric.

notes.heading: Recording and Presenting Data
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Results are recorded in a table as they are collected, then presented in a graph or chart so patterns become easier to see.

🔑 How it works — results tables
• Draw the table before you start the experiment, using a pencil and ruler.
• Put the independent variable in the first column and the dependent variable in the following columns.
• Give every column a heading, with the unit in the heading (e.g. "Time in seconds") — never write units next to individual readings.
• Leave room for repeat readings and a mean.

🔑 How it works — choosing a chart
• Line graph: use when both the independent and dependent variables are continuous. The independent variable goes on the horizontal ($x$) axis, the dependent variable on the vertical ($y$) axis.
• Bar chart: use when the independent variable is categoric or discrete; leave a gap between the bars.
• Pie chart: use to show proportions of a whole, usually as percentages, for discrete or categoric data.

💡 Worked Example
Measuring the mass of salt that dissolves in water at six different temperatures gives two continuous variables, so a line graph is correct. Plot temperature on the $x$-axis and mass dissolved on the $y$-axis, then draw a line of best fit — a smooth line passing through the middle of the points, with roughly half the points above it and half below. Ignore any outliers when drawing it.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Choose a simple scale that uses most of the graph paper.
• Label both axes with the variable AND its unit.
• A line of best fit shows the trend; it does not have to pass through every point.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Joining the points dot-to-dot. In science, a line of best fit (straight or a smooth curve) shows the underlying trend and averages out the scatter in the data.

notes.heading: Analysing Results, Conclusions and Evaluation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
• The mean of repeat readings is found by adding the results together and dividing by the number of results.
• Accurate results are close to the true value; precise results are repeat readings that are close to each other.
• Results are repeatable if YOU get similar values when you repeat the experiment, and reproducible if SOMEONE ELSE gets similar values.
• A conclusion states what you found out and whether it supports your hypothesis; an evaluation judges the quality of your results and method and suggests improvements.

🔑 How it works
Taking repeat readings and calculating a mean makes your data more accurate, because it reduces the effect of random error — unpredictable differences between readings that can cause an outlier (a result very different from the others). A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount, for example a balance that was not reset to zero, and it makes results less accurate no matter how many repeats you take. Once the data is analysed, a good conclusion: 1. describes the relationship ("as temperature increased, the time decreased"), 2. links back to the hypothesis, and 3. explains the findings using scientific knowledge. An evaluation then asks: are there outliers or a big spread? Were enough readings taken over a wide enough range? Was it a valid test — were control variables really kept constant? Could better apparatus reduce the spread? Finish by suggesting specific improvements, such as more repeats or more accurate equipment.

💡 Worked Example
Three timings for a reaction are $5.2$ s, $5.6$ s and $5.7$ s.
$$\text{mean} = \dfrac{5.2 + 5.6 + 5.7}{3} = \dfrac{16.5}{3} = 5.5 \text{ s}$$
If the third reading had been $8.7$ s instead, it would be an outlier: repeat it, and if the repeat is close to $5.2$ and $5.6$, leave the outlier out of the mean. A conclusion might read: "The reaction was faster in more concentrated acid, which supports the hypothesis that more particles in the same volume collide more often." An evaluation could note that timings were judged by eye, so repeat readings or a light sensor would improve accuracy.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always check for outliers before calculating a mean — exclude them.
• A parallax error (reading a scale from an angle instead of at eye level) is a common random error; systematic errors cannot be fixed by repeating — the equipment or technique must be corrected.
• A conclusion is about WHAT you found; an evaluation is about HOW MUCH you trust it.
• Improvements must be specific — "be more careful" is not an improvement.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Including an outlier in the mean. One outlier of $8.7$ s with $5.2$ s and $5.6$ s pulls the mean up to $6.5$ s, which does not represent the data at all.

flashcards.definition: The variable that is deliberately changed during an experiment.
flashcards.example: Changing the concentration of acid to see how it affects the rate of reaction.

flashcards.definition: The variable that is measured in an experiment; it may change in response to the independent variable.
flashcards.example: The time taken for a strip of magnesium to disappear in acid.

flashcards.definition: A variable that is kept the same so that only the independent variable can affect the dependent variable.
flashcards.example: Using the same volume of acid and the same size of magnesium strip in every test.

flashcards.definition: An idea, based on scientific knowledge, that explains how or why something happens and can be tested by experiment.
flashcards.example: Reactions go faster when reacting particles collide more often.

flashcards.definition: A statement of what you expect to happen in an experiment if the hypothesis is correct, linking the independent and dependent variables.
flashcards.example: If the acid temperature increases, the time for the magnesium to disappear will decrease.
Concentrated hydrochloric acid is a hazard because it can burn skin.

flashcards.definition: The chance that a hazard will actually cause harm.
flashcards.example: Wearing goggles reduces the risk of acid splashing into your eyes.

flashcards.definition: Numeric data that can take any value within a range.
flashcards.example: Temperature, time, mass and volume are all continuous.

flashcards.definition: Data whose values are words or labels rather than numbers.
flashcards.example: The colour of a precipitate: red, blue or green.

flashcards.definition: A result that is very different from the other repeat readings; it is left out when calculating the mean.
flashcards.example: Readings of $5.2$ s, $5.6$ s and $9.1$ s — the $9.1$ s reading is an outlier.

flashcards.definition: A result is accurate if it is close to the true value.
flashcards.example: Calculating a mean of repeat readings, ignoring outliers, gives a more accurate result.

flashcards.definition: Results are precise if repeat readings are close to each other.
flashcards.example: Timings of $5.2$ s, $5.3$ s and $5.2$ s are precise; $5.2$ s, $6.9$ s and $4.1$ s are not.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the temperature of hydrochloric acid affects the time taken for magnesium ribbon to disappear. Which is the independent variable?
choices: The time taken for the magnesium to disappear
The temperature of the hydrochloric acid
The mass of the magnesium ribbon
The volume of acid used
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one deliberately changed — here the temperature of the acid. The time is dependent (it is measured), while mass and volume are control variables.

questions.stem: In an experiment on how the concentration of acid affects the rate of reaction, what is the dependent variable most likely to be?
choices: The concentration of the acid
The size of the conical flask
The time taken for the reaction to finish
The temperature of the room
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what you measure in response to the change — the time for the reaction to finish. Concentration is independent; flask size and room temperature should be controlled.

questions.stem: Why must control variables be kept the same during an experiment?
choices: So that only the independent variable can affect the dependent variable
So that the experiment finishes more quickly
So that the results table is easier to draw
So that fewer measurements are needed
questions.explanation: Keeping control variables constant makes the test valid: any change in the dependent variable must then be caused by the independent variable alone.

questions.stem: Which of these is a scientific prediction?
choices: Chemical reactions happen when particles collide
Thermometers should be read at eye level
If the temperature increases, the time for the reaction will decrease
Rate of reaction is an interesting topic
questions.explanation: A prediction states what you expect to happen to the dependent variable when the independent variable changes. The first option is background science, not a prediction.

choices: A list of the apparatus needed for an experiment
The final statement of what the results showed
A testable idea, based on science, that explains how or why something happens
A guess that cannot be checked by an experiment
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is an explanation grounded in scientific knowledge that can be tested experimentally — it is much more than an uncheckable guess.

questions.stem: What is the best FIRST step when planning an experiment?
choices: Draw a graph of the expected results
Decide on the question you want to answer
Calculate the mean of the results
Write the conclusion
questions.explanation: Planning starts with the question to be answered. Variables, prediction, equipment and method all follow from it; graphs, means and conclusions come after the data is collected.

questions.stem: Why should a method be written as numbered steps naming the apparatus and quantities used?
choices: So that it takes up less space in a lab book
So that no results table is needed
So that the teacher can mark it more easily
So that someone else can repeat the experiment and get similar results
questions.explanation: A method is a set of instructions: precise steps with named apparatus and quantities let another scientist reproduce the experiment and check the results.

questions.stem: Concentrated hydrochloric acid can burn skin. In scientific language, the acid itself is best described as a...
choices: risk
hazard
precaution
control variable
questions.explanation: A hazard is something that can cause harm, like the acid. The risk is the chance of it actually causing harm, and a precaution is an action taken to reduce that risk.

questions.stem: Which action reduces the RISK of harm when heating a liquid in a test tube?
choices: Filling the test tube to the top so it heats evenly
Pointing the test tube away from people and wearing goggles
Heating it as quickly as possible over the roaring flame
Holding the test tube in your hand to feel the temperature
questions.explanation: Pointing the tube away and wearing goggles are precautions that reduce the chance of hot liquid harming anyone. The other options all increase the risk.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of continuous data?
choices: The number of bubbles produced in one minute
The colour of the flame during heating
The temperature of the water
The type of metal used
questions.explanation: Temperature can take any value within a range, so it is continuous. A count of bubbles is discrete, while colour and metal type are categoric.

questions.stem: Which set contains only categoric data?
choices: red, blue, green
$12$ bubbles, $18$ bubbles, $25$ bubbles
questions.explanation: Categoric data takes word values, such as colours. Masses and temperatures are continuous numbers, and bubble counts are discrete numbers.

questions.stem: A student measures the mass of salt that dissolves in water at five different temperatures. What is the best way to present these results?
choices: A pie chart
A bar chart with gaps between the bars
A line graph
A written paragraph describing each result
questions.explanation: Both temperature and mass dissolved are continuous variables, so a line graph with a line of best fit is the correct choice.

questions.stem: On a line graph of experimental results, which variable is plotted on the horizontal (x) axis?
choices: The dependent variable
The independent variable
The control variable
The variable with the largest values
questions.explanation: The independent variable (the one you changed) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (the one you measured) goes on the y-axis.

questions.stem: Three repeat timings for a reaction are $4.2$ s, $4.5$ s and $4.8$ s. What is the mean time?
questions.explanation: The mean is the total divided by the number of results: $(4.2 + 4.5 + 4.8) \div 3 = 13.5 \div 3 = 4.5$ s. There are no outliers to exclude.

questions.stem: A balance reads $0.2$ g even with nothing on it, so every mass recorded in an experiment is $0.2$ g too high. What kind of error is this?
choices: A random error
An outlier
A parallax error
A systematic error
questions.explanation: Every reading is shifted by the same amount ($0.2$ g), which is the signature of a systematic error. Repeating readings will not fix it — the balance must be reset to zero.
